name: A Survey on the Feedback Mechanism of LLM-based AI Agents
authors: Zhipeng Liu, Xuefeng Bai, Kehai Chen, et al. (Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen; Peng Cheng Laboratory; Central South University)
code_url: https://github.com/kevinson7515/Agents-Feedback-Mechanisms (curated paper list, not a method implementation)
reflection_type: Survey covering the full spectrum of feedback/reflection types it taxonomizes: verbal-self-critique (internal feedback, e.g. Self-Refine, Reflexion), tool-verified/external (compiler, search engine, game API, world-model feedback), multi-agent-debate (collaborative and adversarial), and human feedback (instructional, corrective, preference). As an analysis/survey artifact it has no single reflection_type of its own.
feedback_source: Survey organizes feedback by source into four top-level categories: internal/self-generated (intra-task and inter-task), external-tool (compiler/interpreter, search engine, game API, world model, environment reward), multi-agent (peer agents in collaborative or adversarial setups), and human (instructional, corrective, preference). It synthesizes across all of these rather than proposing one.
iteration_structure: Survey-level synthesis. Reviewed methods span single-shot and iterative-refine (Self-Refine, Reflexion, Voyager); the survey explicitly tags each representative work with an 'Iteration (or not)' column in Table 1. No new iteration structure is proposed.
reflection_object: As a survey, it discusses reflection over many objects: output content (Self-Refine), reasoning chain (CoT-based internal feedback, SelfCheck), action trajectory (ReAct, Reflexion, ExpeL inter-task experience), reusable skill/workflow (Voyager skill library), and model weights (RLHF/RL-from-compiler-feedback methods like StepCoder, CodeRL, Retroformer). The survey's unifying frame is the 'feedback module' acting on the agent's prior decisions and actions across perception/planning/memory/action modules.
requires_training: Survey covering both training-free in-context methods (ReAct, Self-Refine, Reflexion verbal RL, ExpeL, AutoGuide use ICL with no weight updates) and gradient-update methods (RLHF/InstructGPT, RL-from-compiler-feedback StepCoder/CodeRL, policy-gradient Retroformer, preference learning DPO-style/Christiano-style RLHF). It does not itself train a model.
reward_or_critic_model: Survey enumerates many improvement-signal sources: self-as-judge (internal feedback), external verifiable signals (compiler success, task completion, environment reward), separate feedback/critic models, multi-agent peer evaluation, LLM-as-judge / Agent-as-a-judge, and human reward/preference models. It notes LLM-as-judge suffers positional bias, verbosity bias, and weakness on math.
distillation_target: Survey discusses several reusable artifacts that reflection can be distilled into: episodic-memory (Reflexion stores self-reflections; Generative Agents memory stream), reusable-skill/workflow (Voyager skill library), prompt/guideline (AutoGuide context-aware guidelines), and model-weights (RL/SFT methods such as StepCoder, Retroformer, RLHF). No single target is prescribed.
emergent_vs_engineered: Predominantly covers prompt/scaffold-engineered reflective behavior (Reflexion, Self-Refine, ReAct, Voyager, multi-agent debate), framed as designed feedback modules rather than RL-emergent reflection. The survey predates/does not center R1-style RL-emergent 'aha' reasoning; reflection is treated as an explicitly engineered module within a five-module agent framework.
memory_type: Survey covers the memory dimension explicitly: it defines a memory module with long-term memory (stable knowledge) and short-term memory (real-time task info), and reviewed methods use scratchpad/short-term memory, long-term-episodic memory (Reflexion, Generative Agents, RAP), and skill-library memory (Voyager). Tightly coupled with the feedback module in its unified framework.
memory_persistence: Survey spans within-episode (intra-task feedback, Self-Refine), cross-episode/cross-task (inter-task feedback: Reflexion, ExpeL, Retroformer transfer experience across tasks via stored trajectories and reflections), with cross-task experience integration highlighted as a key strength of inter-task feedback. No production cross-session deployment focus.
memory_curation_mechanism: Survey notes that inter-task feedback 'demands substantial memory to store historical task experience' and that the central challenge is combining intra- and inter-task feedback efficiently. Reviewed methods use append-style episodic stores (Reflexion), retrieval over similar past trajectories (ExpeL, RAP), and curated guideline generation/selection (AutoGuide). No unified curation scheme is prescribed.
error_localization_granularity: Survey-level; spans holistic/outcome-level (most QA and success-rate benchmarks), response-level (Self-Refine output revision), step-level (SelfCheck per-step reasoning checks; DevAI evaluates each stage; AdaPlanner code-splitting), and agent-level (multi-agent feedback attributing roles/responsibilities). It critiques outcome-only benchmarks for ignoring the reasoning process.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: Both, and this is an explicit organizing axis of the survey: internal feedback is sub-divided into intra-task (refine within current task, e.g. ReAct, Self-Refine) and inter-task (transfer experience across tasks, e.g. Reflexion, ExpeL, Retroformer, RAP). Discussion section contrasts their complementary strengths/limits.
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: Survey covers both: mid-trajectory recovery (Voyager combining execution errors and self-validation to repair programs in-flight; ReAct interleaving reasoning and acting; QueryAgent self-correction via environmental feedback) and post-hoc/avoidance via retrospection in the next episode (Reflexion, ExpeL using prior-task experience to avoid repeating mistakes).
task_domains: Survey spans QA/reasoning, code generation, web-navigation, embodied/games (virtual worlds, robotics), tool-use, dialogue, multi-agent collaboration, machine translation, financial reasoning, social simulation, and general decision-making/alignment.
benchmarks: Survey catalogs benchmarks by domain (Table 2): Reasoning (HotpotQA, ScienceQA, StrategyQA); Virtual World (ALFWorld, IGLU, MineRL/Minecraft); Embodied Action (Franka Kitchen, Meta-World, RT-X); Web Navigation (WebShop, WebArena, Mind2Web, WebVoyager); Code Generation (MBPP, HumanEval, SWE-bench, DevAI); Social Simulation (SocialBench, SocKET); Tool Usage (ToolBench, TravelPlanner, ToolEyes); Multi-agent Collaboration (RoCoBench, PARTNR, VillagerBench); Machine Translation (WMT, FLORES-200); Financial (FiQA_SA, FinQA); Multidimensional (AgentBench).
headline_result: Survey (no single headline number of its own). Its experimental comparison (Table 3, on HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop, with some results borrowed from ExpeL and AutoGuide) qualitatively reports: ReAct gives limited gains on complex reasoning (HotpotQA, StrategyQA) but strong performance on sequential decision tasks (ALFWorld, WebShop); Reflexion further improves ALFWorld via iterative learning, with the largest jump between the first and second trials; ExpeL and AutoGuide add stability on long-horizon dynamic tasks. Specific numeric deltas are not legibly recoverable from the OCR of the proceedings PDF.
baselines: In its comparative analysis the survey contrasts non-learning methods (CoT, Act, ReAct) against iterative-learning feedback methods (Reflexion, ExpeL, AutoGuide, AdaPlanner) and against traditional scalar-reward reinforcement learning, evaluated on HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and WebShop.
gains_vs_baseline: Reported only qualitatively: iterative feedback methods (Reflexion, ExpeL, AutoGuide) yield greater stability and accuracy than single-run CoT/Act/ReAct on long-horizon dynamic tasks; Reflexion's largest improvement on ALFWorld occurs between trial 1 and trial 2. The survey argues verbal/linguistic feedback (Reflexion) beats scalar-reward RL on trial-and-error learning, efficiency (no fine-tuning), feedback specificity, and interpretability. Exact numeric deltas are [uncertain] from the available PDF OCR.
compute_cost_profile: Not quantified numerically. The survey qualitatively argues in-context verbal-feedback methods (Reflexion) are more data- and compute-efficient than scalar-reward RL because they avoid fine-tuning the LLM, and warns that multi-agent feedback sharply raises computational demands and communication overhead as agent count grows. No token/API-call multipliers are reported.
known_limitations: Survey identifies six open challenges: (1) real-time feedback and scaling multi-agent systems (rising compute, communication overhead, lack of standardized protocols such as MCP/A2A/ANP/Agora); (2) integrating multimodal feedback (cross-modal alignment); (3) meta-learning adaptive feedback (feedback conflicts, overfitting to evolving user needs); (4) explainability/transparency of feedback mechanisms; (5) sim-to-real transfer for embodied agents; (6) inherent LLM/VLM limitations (hallucination, bias). It also flags ethical bias risks in human feedback (gender, race, culture).
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: Survey makes external-vs-internal feedback a central axis. It notes external feedback (compiler, search, environment reward, world model) gives insights self-improvement cannot, but its effectiveness 'is highly dependent on the quality and relevance of external information.' It frames internal/self-feedback as limited and recommends external tools, multi-agent debate, RAG cross-validation, and world models to correct hallucinations and reasoning errors.
self_correction_efficacy: task-dependent. Survey reports intra-task self-refinement enables rapid optimization but is limited by its task-specific nature, while external and multi-agent feedback are needed to correct hallucinations and reasoning errors that pure self-feedback misses; multi-agent negotiation can also converge on incorrect consensus. Efficacy is framed as contingent on feedback source quality rather than uniformly net-positive.
calibration_effect: not-measured. The survey does not analyze calibration/overconfidence ('reasoning tax') of reasoning models; it predates that lens and focuses on feedback taxonomy, hallucination, and bias rather than calibration metrics.
failure_attribution_capability: n/a (survey). It does not perform formal failure attribution, but discusses failure modes qualitatively: multi-agent systems risk uncontrolled discussions (mitigated by coordination agents like ChatLLM), reward misalignment among agents (CollabQ), convergence on incorrect consensus (PRD peer-ranking), LLM hallucination/bias, and option bias in QA benchmarks.
failure_mode_addressed: Discusses failure modes including hallucination/factual error, reasoning errors, multi-agent reward misalignment and conflict, uncontrolled debate, incorrect-consensus convergence (analogous to MAST inter-agent misalignment), QA option/positional bias, LLM-as-judge verbosity/positional bias, and sim-to-real transfer failure. Proposed fixes: dedicated coordination agents, peer-ranking, RAG cross-validation, world models, multi-agent debate.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: No new dataset or benchmark released. The survey releases a curated, continually-updated paper list at https://github.com/kevinson7515/Agents-Feedback-Mechanisms (README organizes works by feedback category and benchmarks).
builds_on: Synthesizes and builds on prior surveys (Wang et al. 2023 'A survey on LLM-based autonomous agents'; Xi et al. 'The rise and potential of LLM-based agents'; Pan et al. 2024 and Madaan et al. self-correction surveys; Cheng et al. 2024; Durante et al. 2024 Agent AI) and foundational methods it taxonomizes: ReAct, Reflexion, Self-Refine, Voyager, ExpeL, MetaGPT, Multi-agent Debate (Du et al.), InstructGPT/RLHF, StepCoder, Generative Agents.
reasoning_model_native: no — the survey is organized around engineered feedback modules and verbal/RL feedback for general LLM agents; it does not specifically target o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflection.
sample_efficiency: Not quantified. The survey qualitatively argues verbal-feedback methods (Reflexion) are more data/compute efficient than scalar-reward RL (no fine-tuning needed) and notes Reflexion's main ALFWorld gain appears within the first 1-2 trials, but reports no formal sample-efficiency numbers.
